title: GEOGloWS Evaluation for Nepal Flood AA Framework
text:
Purpose
This book evaluates the GEOGloWS River Forecast System (v2) as a potential data source for Nepal’s flood anticipatory action (AA) trigger framework.
The existing framework relies on:

GloFAS (ECMWF/Copernicus) — reanalysis and reforecast data for discharge thresholds and trigger calibration
DHM (Department of Hydrology and Meteorology, Nepal) — observed water level data from gauge stations
Google GRRR — experimental streamflow reforecast and reanalysis from Google Cloud

GEOGloWS offers a complementary global streamflow service with some distinct advantages — most notably an 86-year retrospective simulation (1940–present) and a free, unauthenticated API. This evaluation investigates whether and how GEOGloWS data can strengthen the trigger framework.

title: GEOGloWS Evaluation for Nepal Flood AA Framework
text:
Key Finding
GEOGloWS does not provide reforecasts (hindcasts). The forecast archive extends only ~2 months. This means it cannot be used for the lead-time-dependent skill assessment and trigger calibration that the AA framework requires. However, the long retrospective record and built-in bias correction tools make it valuable for validation and as a complementary real-time signal.

title: 1  GEOGloWS Overview
text:
1.1 What is GEOGloWS?
GEOGloWS (Group on Earth Observations Global Water Sustainability) is a GEO initiative that provides a global streamflow forecasting and historical simulation service. The flagship product is the GEOGloWS ECMWF Streamflow Service, a partnership between GEO, ECMWF, and Brigham Young University (BYU).
The service aims to give every country access to hydrological forecasts, particularly countries that lack national forecasting infrastructure. Version 2 was released in 2024 with significant improvements to the river network and data access infrastructure.

title: 1  GEOGloWS Overview
text:
1.2 Model Architecture
The system has two components:

1.2.1 Forecasts

Meteorological forcing: ECMWF IFS (Integrated Forecasting System) ensemble weather forecasts provide runoff inputs
Routing model: RAPID (Routing Application for Parallel computation of Discharge) routes runoff through the global river network
River network: TDX-Hydro — derived from TanDEM-X 90m DEM, approximately 6.8 million river reaches globally
Ensemble members: 52 (51 perturbed + 1 high-resolution control)
Forecast lead time: 15 days
Temporal resolution: Hourly (3-hourly for ensemble members, hourly for high-res)
Update frequency: Daily



1.2.2 Retrospective Simulation

Meteorological forcing: ERA5 reanalysis (ECMWF’s global atmospheric reanalysis)
Period: 1940 to present — this is substantially longer than GloFAS (1979–present)
Temporal resolution: Hourly (also available as daily, monthly, yearly aggregates)
Return periods: Pre-computed for 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100-year levels using Log-Pearson III distribution



1.2.3 Critical Conceptual Note: Retrospective vs Reforecast
This distinction is fundamental to understanding what GEOGloWS can and cannot do for trigger calibration:
Retrospective (what GEOGloWS has): A single deterministic time series of “what the model thinks happened” from 1940–present. It uses ERA5 reanalysis — essentially observed weather run through the routing model after the fact. There is no forecast uncertainty because the meteorological input is already known. You get one discharge value per timestep.
Reforecast (what GloFAS has, GEOGloWS does not): For each historical date, the forecast system is re-run as if standing on that date not knowing the future. For example, for July 15 2015, you get an N-member ensemble forecast with multiple leadtime steps — and you can compare what it predicted at 3-day and 7-day lead against what actually happened.
The retrospective is the answer key. The reforecast is the student’s exam papers. You need both to grade forecast skill. For AA trigger calibration — where the question is “if X% of ensemble members exceed the threshold at 3-day lead, should we trigger?” — you need reforecasts to calibrate X%. The retrospective alone cannot answer this.
GEOGloWS’s forecast archive extends only ~2 months back, far too short for trigger calibration.

title: 2  Spatial Matching
text:
2.1 The Sensitivity Problem
Mapping physical gauge stations to GEOGloWS river reach IDs is the first practical challenge. GEOGloWS uses the TDX-Hydro river network, where each reach has a unique 9-digit integer ID. The geoglows package and REST API provide tools to find reach IDs from coordinates — but they are surprisingly sensitive to small coordinate shifts.
The REST API’s getriverid endpoint returns the nearest river reach outlet to a given lat/lon. But “nearest” can snap to a tiny tributary instead of the main stem if the coordinates are slightly off.
We tested this at Chatara on the Koshi river. The code to reproduce:

title: 2  Spatial Matching
text:
2.4 Recommendations for Spatial Matching

Never trust latlon_to_river() or getriverid blindly — always verify the return periods or upstream area of the matched reach make hydrological sense.
For large rivers, query the metadata table by upstream area — this is more reliable than coordinate snapping.
Cross-reference with known discharge magnitudes — if you have GloFAS or observed return periods, use them to validate the matched reach.
The REST getriverid endpoint is faster than latlon_to_river() — the latter downloads a ~100MB metadata table.

title: 3  Return Period Comparison
text:
3.1 Data Sources and Methods
Return period thresholds are central to the AA trigger framework — they define what constitutes a “significant” flood event. Different data sources compute return periods using different methods, distributional assumptions, and underlying data, producing notably different threshold values.
The GEOGloWS retrospective covers 86 years vs GloFAS’s 44 years. A longer record should produce more stable extreme value estimates, but the underlying hydrological model also differs (RAPID routing-only vs LISFLOOD full land surface).

title: 3  Return Period Comparison
text:
3.4 Why the Difference?
Several factors contribute to the divergence:

Different distributions: Log-Pearson III (GEOGloWS) vs Gumbel (GloFAS). Log-Pearson III has a heavier tail which can produce higher extreme value estimates.
Different record lengths: 86 years (GEOGloWS) vs 44 years (GloFAS). The longer GEOGloWS record may capture rarer extreme events that the GloFAS period misses.
Different hydrological models: RAPID routes ECMWF runoff through a vector river network. LISFLOOD (GloFAS) is a full land-surface model with calibration against ~2,000+ gauges. The uncalibrated RAPID model may overestimate peak flows.
Different river delineation: TDX-Hydro reaches vs GloFAS grid cells. The contributing area of the matched reach may differ between systems.
Different spatial representation: The GEOGloWS river_id we matched may not correspond to the exact same point on the river as the GloFAS grid cell.

title: 3  Return Period Comparison
text:
3.5 Implications for the AA Framework
If GEOGloWS return periods were used directly as trigger thresholds, they would produce fewer triggers than GloFAS thresholds (higher bar to clear). However, this comparison is between return periods derived from different models — the forecast discharge magnitudes also differ. The meaningful comparison is event-level: does GEOGloWS flag the same flood events as actually observed? This is explored in Chapter 5.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(14, 8), sharex=False)

for i, (key, station) in enumerate(STATIONS.items()):
    ax = axes[i]

    # GEOGloWS
    geo = geoglows[key]
    ax.plot(geo.index, geo["discharge"],
            color="#888888", alpha=0.5, linewidth=0.3, label="GEOGloWS")

    # GloFAS
    gf = glofas_df[station.dhm_column]
    ax.plot(gf.index, gf.values,
            color="#1f77b4", alpha=0.7, linewidth=0.3, label="GloFAS")

    # GRRR
    if key in grrr:
        gr = grrr[key]
        ax.plot(gr.index, gr["streamflow"],
                color="#2ca02c", alpha=0.7, linewidth=0.3, label="GRRR")

    # Return period lines
    ax.axhline(station.glofas_rp2, color="#d62728", linestyle="--",
               alpha=0.5, label=f"GloFAS RP2 ({station.glofas_rp2:,})")

# Get unique event dates (collapse consecutive exceedance days into events)
def collapse_to_events(dates, gap_days=7):
    """Collapse consecutive/nearby dates into distinct events."""
    if len(dates) == 0:
        return pd.DatetimeIndex([])
    dates = dates.sort_values()
    events = [dates[0]]
    for d in dates[1:]:
        if (d - events[-1]).days > gap_days:
            events.append(d)
    return pd.DatetimeIndex(events)

5.7 Discussion
Key observations from the event matching:

GloFAS at RP2 had extremely high false alarm rates — 33 false alarms at Chatara, 95 at Chisapani. The GloFAS RP2 thresholds appear too low relative to DHM danger levels.
GEOGloWS RP2 thresholds are much higher (14,459 vs 8,113 m³/s at Chatara), which should produce fewer false alarms — but potentially at the cost of missed events.
The fundamental challenge is that DHM measures water level (meters) while models produce discharge (m³/s). Without a rating curve, the comparison is indirect: we’re checking whether the model’s “extreme event” aligns with the observed “extreme event,” not whether the magnitudes match.

title: 6  Bias Correction
text:
6.1 Available Methods
The geoglows package includes a bias correction module (geoglows.bias) with several methods. This chapter explores what’s available and applies the methods that don’t require observed discharge data (since DHM provides water level, not discharge).
The geoglows.bias module provides three approaches:
Since DHM data is water level (meters), not discharge (m³/s), we cannot directly use correct_historical(). The SFDC method is the primary option — it uses pre-computed correction scalars derived from the SABER (Statistical Adjustment By Empirical Regression) approach.

6.2 SFDC Bias Correction
The SFDC method works by:

Computing the simulated flow duration curve (FDC) for each month
Looking up pre-computed scalar factors that map simulated FDC percentiles to bias-corrected values
Applying these scalars to adjust the simulated discharge

title: 6  Bias Correction
text:
6.5 Limitations

SFDC scalars are not available for all rivers. The pre-computed correction factors depend on having nearby observed data in the SABER database. Some rivers may not have coverage.
correct_historical() requires observed discharge, not water level. If a rating curve for Chatara or Chisapani becomes available, this method could produce better results than SFDC.
Bias correction adjusts magnitudes but does not improve event timing. If the model misses an event (wrong rainfall distribution in ERA5), no bias correction will fix that.

title: 7  Assessment
text: 7.1 Summary of Findings

title: 7  Assessment
text:
7.1.1 What GEOGloWS Provides

86-year retrospective (1940–present) vs GloFAS’s 44-year record (1979–present). This is the single most valuable asset — nearly double the historical record for extreme value analysis.
52-member ensemble forecasts with 15-day lead time, freely accessible via Python API with no authentication.
Pre-computed return periods (2–100 year) using Log-Pearson III distribution.
Built-in bias correction (SFDC/SABER method) that doesn’t require local observed discharge data.
Global reach-level resolution (~6.8 million river reaches) — much denser spatial coverage than GloFAS’s gridded output.



7.1.2 What GEOGloWS Cannot Provide

No reforecasts/hindcasts. The forecast archive extends only ~2 months. This is the critical gap — the AA framework needs reforecasts to calibrate trigger thresholds at specific lead times (3-day action, 7-day readiness). Without reforecasts, we cannot compute exceedance probability skill metrics or determine optimal ensemble agreement thresholds.
Spatial matching is fragile. The getriverid API is sensitive to coordinates — a 0.07° shift mapped to a completely different reach. For the Karnali, coordinate-based lookup failed entirely; we had to query the metadata table by upstream contributing area.

7.2 Recommendation
GEOGloWS should not replace GloFAS or Google GRRR for trigger calibration — the missing reforecasts make this impossible. However, it is worth incorporating as:

7.2.1 1. Validation Dataset
The 86-year retrospective provides a longer historical record for return period estimation and event catalog construction. Cross-referencing GEOGloWS events with GloFAS and DHM observations triangulates biases.


7.2.2 2. Complementary Real-Time Signal
Once triggers are calibrated using GloFAS/GRRR reforecasts, GEOGloWS’s 52-member ensemble forecast can serve as an independent confirmation signal. If both GloFAS and GEOGloWS forecasts exceed their respective thresholds, confidence in the trigger activation increases.


7.2.3 3. Bias Correction Benchmark
The SFDC method provides a globally-derived bias correction that doesn’t require local gauge data. Comparing SFDC-corrected GEOGloWS against GloFAS reanalysis can help quantify model biases.
